title: Why mint feels cold
question: Why does mint feel icy without making anything colder?
takeaway: Mint does not lower temperature. Menthol activates cold receptors, so your brain reads the signal as cold.
mechanism: Menthol activates the TRPM8 cold receptor in the mouth and skin.

title: Why cold drains phone batteries
question: Why does phone battery drop faster in the cold?
takeaway: Cold slows ion movement, voltage drops, and the phone reports less battery.
mechanism: Low temperature increases resistance inside a lithium-ion battery. Ions move more slowly, so voltage falls under load and the phone reads that lower voltage as less remaining charge. Some apparent battery can return after warming.

title: The science of caffeine
question: How does caffeine trick your brain into feeling alert?
takeaway: Caffeine does not give the brain energy. It blocks adenosine signals that normally make you feel sleepy.
mechanism: Caffeine crosses into the brain and binds to adenosine receptors without activating them, reducing the sleepy signal and making alertness feel stronger.

title: Why airplane windows are round
question: Why are airplane windows rounded instead of square?
takeaway: Rounded windows spread stress more evenly, while sharp square corners can concentrate stress and increase crack risk.
mechanism: Cabin pressure pushes outward on the fuselage. Curved window edges distribute that stress instead of focusing it at sharp corners.

title: Why brain freeze happens
question: Why does cold food cause forehead pain?
takeaway: Brain freeze is not pain inside the brain. Cold in the mouth triggers nerve signals that the brain interprets as forehead pain.
mechanism: Cold touches the roof of the mouth, blood vessels react quickly, and the trigeminal nerve carries a referred pain signal toward the forehead.

title: Why glass is transparent
question: Why can visible light pass through glass?
takeaway: Glass is transparent because visible light usually does not have the right energy to be absorbed by its atomic structure.
mechanism: The electronic structure of glass leaves a large energy gap for visible wavelengths, so visible light passes through while some ultraviolet and infrared light are absorbed.

title: Leaves breathe through tiny pores
question: How do leaves take in carbon dioxide without losing too much water?
takeaway: Leaves use stomata to let CO₂ in for photosynthesis, but open pores also let water vapor escape.
mechanism: Stomata open and close to balance carbon gain with water saving, allowing gas exchange while limiting water loss.
